To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) a long prime is more likely to be confused with the target, but (b) a long prime can be discounted more than a short one, and (c) the relative strength of these effects can be manipulated by varying the salience of the prime.

(1) the magnitude of primed repetition effects can vary dramatically as a function of prime duration; (2) these changes in priming magnitude are not simply due to changes in prime salience; (3) the effects of prime salience and prime duration can be dissociated; (4) these findings are predicted by a computational model of repetition priming based on the interaction of source confusion and discounting.
